extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners (attorneys and agents), respondents in USPTO disciplinary/reciprocal proceedings, and USPTO enforcement/adjudicative staff
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedures the USPTO applies when deciding whether to impose discipline identical to a State's public disciplinary sanction (e.g., disbarment) under 37 C.F.R. § 11.24, including the limited scope of review and the burdens on the respondent. Applies to reciprocal exclusion/suspension/reprimand of practitioners before the USPTO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal discipline standard under 37 C.F.R. § 11.24
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO Director shall impose the identical public censure, public reprimand, probation, disbarment, suspension, or disciplinary disqualification unless the practitioner clearly and convincingly demonstrates, and the USPTO Director finds there is a genuine issue of material fact that: (i) The procedure elsewhere was so lacking in notice or opportunity to be heard as to constitute a deprivation of due process; (ii) There was such infirmity of proof establishing the conduct as to give rise to the clear conviction that the Office could not, consistently with its duty, accept as final the conclusion on that subject; (iii) The imposition of the same public censure, public reprimand, probation, disbarment, suspension or disciplinary disqualification by the Office would result in grave injustice; or (iv) Any argument that the practitioner was not publicly censured, publicly reprimanded, placed on probation, disbarred, suspended or disciplinarily disqualified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the controlling regulatory test; the quoted four factors are the only means to avoid imposing identical discipline under § 11.24. The practitioner bears the burden to clearly and convincingly demonstrate a genuine issue of material fact as to at least one factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption from Selling v. Radford (state disbarment presumption)
rubrics_metrics.description: A state disbarment creates a federal-level presumption that imposition of reciprocal discipline is proper (Selling v. Radford).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondent must overcome this presumption by establishing one of the § 11.24(d)(1) / Selling infirmities by clear and convincing evidence. Courts and the USPTO apply a narrow standard of review in reciprocal discipline cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof: clear and convincing evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: In reciprocal discipline proceedings the respondent attorney's burden is to demonstrate, by clear and convincing evidence, that one of the Selling elements (due process deprivation, infirmity of proof, or grave injustice) precludes reciprocal discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision cites case law (e.g., In re Kramer, In re Friedman) emphasizing that the burden is narrow and difficult to meet; mere assertions or documentation of rehabilitation do not satisfy the burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of USPTO review: extremely limited; not a de novo review
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO's review in reciprocal discipline is 'extremely limited' and does not permit the Office to sit as a court of review to discover error in the state proceedings; the Office examines the state record only for the specific infirmities identified in Selling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authorities (e.g., Selling, Shippey, Surrick, Kramer, Roman) make clear the USPTO will not retry the misconduct, reconsider the sanction de novo, or substitute its judgment on the underlying factual determinations unless one of the narrow infirmities is shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deprivation of due process criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid reciprocal discipline under § 11.24(d)(1)(i), the practitioner must show the state procedure was so lacking in notice or opportunity to be heard as to constitute a deprivation of due process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Due process is satisfied where the respondent had reasonable notice, representation by counsel, opportunity to present evidence, testify, call and cross-examine witnesses, and to seek review; participation and voluntary stipulation weaken a due-process claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infirmity of proof criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid reciprocal discipline under § 11.24(d)(1)(ii), there must be such an infirmity of proof establishing the conduct that the Office could not, consistently with its duty, accept the state court's conclusion as final.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requires showing the evidence supporting the adjudication is so deficient that the Office cannot accept the outcome; mere disagreement with the findings or new materials that do not undermine proof generally will not suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grave injustice criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid reciprocal discipline under § 11.24(d)(1)(iii), the practitioner must clearly and convincingly demonstrate that imposition of the same discipline by the Office would result in a grave injustice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The grave injustice showing is a high standard and focuses on whether the severity of punishment 'fits' the misconduct (i.e., punishment so ill-fitted to adjudicated misconduct that reciprocal discipline would be unjust). Rehabilitation and post-disciplinary activities rarely suffice to show grave injustice in this limited review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rehabilitative evidence generally not dispositive in reciprocal review
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of rehabilitation (medical treatment, restitution payments, professional activities) does not bear on whether reciprocal discipline should be imposed in the limited § 11.24 review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While rehabilitative steps can matter in reinstatement proceedings (e.g., under 37 C.F.R. § 11.60), they do not generally negate the state discipline for purposes of reciprocal exclusion unless they clearly and convincingly show grave injustice—an uncommon outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of stipulation/admission in state proceeding
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner's written stipulation admitting misconduct and agreeing that disbarment is warranted undermines later claims that the state proceeding lacked due process or proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stipulations approved by the state court and consented to with counsel make it difficult to show the Selling infirmities; the USPTO may rely on those stipulations as part of the state record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-litigation vagueness or statutory-interpretation claims insufficient absent state litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that a state statute was vague or unclear (e.g., Cal. Civ. Code § 2944.7) do not defeat reciprocal discipline if the practitioner admitted the violation in the state record and did not prevail on such a challenge in the state proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unrelated post-hoc evidence (e.g., news reports of sponsor misconduct) does not typically render a statute's plain language unclear for purposes of § 11.24 review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required outcomes and mandatory administrative steps upon exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: If reciprocal discipline is imposed, the Director shall order exclusion (e.g., from practice before the USPTO) and take administrative actions such as making public notice (Official Gazette), notifying disciplinary enforcement agencies and courts, dissociating the practitioner's name from any Customer Numbers and PKI certificate, and prohibiting the practitioner from applying for or being added to a USPTO Customer Number until reinstated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Orders will state the effective date and the statutory/regulatory basis (e.g., 35 U.S.C. § 32, 37 C.F.R. § 11.24). The Office will publish a Notice of Exclusion in the Official Gazette and provide notice pursuant to 37 C.F.R. § 11.59.
